extracted.intended_audience: comedians, comedy writers, and critics interested in stagecraft and post-Nanette approaches to standup
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for standup performers and writers on using and subverting traditional joke structures (punchlines, tension/release, self-deprecation) in the mode Hannah Gadsby developed with Nanette and Douglas. Focuses on narrative architecture, ethics of material, and deliberate formal choices like withholding laughter or naming the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the Joke as Trauma Cap
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard joke form ENDS the story at the laugh; this means the comic can never tell the rest of the story. For trauma material, the joke caps the wound — it doesn't heal it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gadsby's argument: comedians sometimes need to refuse the punchline to honor the truth. Use this criterion to decide whether the conventional punchline would prematurely close off necessary emotional or factual material.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Tension Without Release
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke contract: build tension, release with laughter. A new contract: build tension, REFUSE to release, force the audience to sit with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used carefully, refusing release is one of the most powerful tools in the medium. Consider whether withholding the expected laugh serves the material's ethical or rhetorical aims rather than just frustrating the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Self-Deprecation as Self-Harm
rubrics_metrics.description: For marginalized comedians, self-deprecation about identity is humiliation as labor; the audience is being trained to laugh AT the identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether self-deprecating lines extract laughter from the performer's own identity. If so, find alternative ways to be funny that don't center humiliation or require the performer to degrade themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Story Architecture in Douglas
rubrics_metrics.description: Long, didactic frame establishes intellectual trust; visual humor (art history slides) provides recognition + reframe; personal material is interspersed, anchored by the intellectual frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the show's structure permits both essay and joke to coexist: does an intellectual frame create space for personal disclosure and recontextualize moments of humor without defaulting to conventional punchlines?

rubrics_metrics.name: On Naming the Form
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling out the joke structure to the audience can BE the joke. Saying 'I am about to release the tension' — and then not — destabilizes meaningfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meta-declaration of form deliberately and sparingly (works once per show, perhaps twice). Overuse turns the tactic into shtick; evaluate frequency and intentionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: What does the punchline ALLOW you to skip in the story?
rubrics_metrics.description: A reflective question to evaluate whether delivering a punchline truncates further necessary narrative or analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a checkpoint: identify what further context, emotion, or truth would be omitted if the laugh becomes the endpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is that skip serving the audience, or protecting you?
rubrics_metrics.description: A diagnostic question prompting the performer to examine motive: is omission for audience benefit or self-protection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize audience understanding and ethical honesty; if the skip mainly shields the performer, reconsider the punchline or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could withholding the laugh serve the material better here?
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether refusing the expected release (withholding the laugh) strengthens the piece's message or emotional impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference with 'Tension Without Release' — withholding should be purposeful, not gratuitous; test audience reaction in rehearsal but remain faithful to intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you're self-deprecating, are you laughing AT your own identity?
rubrics_metrics.description: A criterion to detect whether self-directed jokes also function as attacks on the performer's identity that train audiences to deride that identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the answer is yes, rework material to avoid extracting laughter from identity-based humiliation; seek reframing, irony, or other targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the form of the show let intellect and laughter coexist?
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the overall structure supports both didactic/analytical elements and comedic beats without one negating the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for devices (frames, visual aids, pacing) that build intellectual trust and allow personal/joke moments to land; ensure the show isn't forced into a single-mode expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have you named the form deliberately, sparingly, or accidentally?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether meta-comments about structure were intentional and appropriately used, or merely accidental and repetitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming the form can be a potent device when deliberate and limited; frequent or accidental naming risks becoming mere shtick and undermining the piece's seriousness.
